name: Fallibility of Perception
what: This subtopic introduces the concept that both visual and gustatory perception are prone to error in normally functioning individuals. It distinguishes between errors occurring at the level of sensation versus errors occurring during the brain's processing and interpretation of sensory information.
why: Understanding that perceptual errors are normal and expected challenges the assumption that our senses give us a perfectly accurate picture of reality. This foundation is essential for making sense of all the specific phenomena studied throughout the chapter.

items.title: I can define fallibility and explain how it applies to perception
items.what: Fallibility is the quality of being prone to error or experiencing difficulties in judgement. Applied to perception, it means that our brain's processing of sensory information can produce inaccurate experiences even when the sensory organs themselves are working normally.
items.why: Recognising that fallibility is a normal feature of perception prevents students from assuming that perceptual errors always indicate a disorder or defect. It frames the entire topic correctly before specific examples are introduced.
items.example: A person with perfect vision still consistently perceives one line in the Muller-Lyer illusion as longer than the other, even after being told they are equal in length. The eye is functioning normally; the error is in the brain's interpretation.

items.title: I can define perceptual distortion and distinguish it from a sensation error
items.what: A perceptual distortion is an error in the judgement or interpretation of sensory stimuli. It differs from a sensation error in that the sensory organs detect information accurately, but the brain misinterprets or misrepresents that information during the perception stage.
items.why: This distinction is critical for exam responses. Many students confuse agnosia, spatial neglect, and illusions with problems in the eye or ear, when in fact the distortion occurs during perception in the brain.
items.example: A patient with visual agnosia can see a toothbrush clearly (normal sensation) but cannot identify what object it is (distortion during perceptual interpretation). The eye is not at fault.

items.title: I can identify the three general sources of visual illusions
items.what: Visual illusions can arise from environmental sources (features of the physical world that make interpretation difficult), physiological sources (biological processes in the eyes or brain that create misleading signals), or psychological sources (personal biases, expectations, and prior learning that shape interpretation).
items.why: Knowing these three categories allows students to correctly classify and explain unfamiliar illusions in exam questions, not just the specific examples studied in class.
items.example: The moon appearing larger near the horizon is an environmental illusion. An afterimage following a bright flash is physiological. Susceptibility to the Muller-Lyer illusion being greater in people raised in built environments is psychological or social.

items.title: I can explain that perceptual distortions occur in healthy brains and do not indicate a malfunction
items.what: Experiencing perceptual distortions, including illusions, synaesthesia, or spatial neglect caused by a lesion, does not mean that the brain is fundamentally broken or that perception is useless. These phenomena demonstrate the dynamic, interpretive nature of perception rather than a catastrophic failure.
items.why: Students need this perspective to write balanced evaluation responses, and it reflects the nuanced scientific understanding that normality and abnormality exist on a continuum.
items.example: Every person with normal vision will be fooled by the Ames room illusion when viewing it through a peephole with one eye, because the room is deliberately designed to exploit the brain's normal visual processing rules.
